study.title: Ezekiel 13 The judgment of God against the religious lie
study.overview: Ezekiel 13 confronts prophets and prophetesthes who spoke of their own hearts instead of the word of the LORD. The chapter shows that the religious lie is not neutral: it deceives the people, promises peace where there is no peace, weakens the righteous and strengthens the wicked. God responds with direct judgment, exposing the falsehood of these messengers and completely undoing the false security they built. The text insists that true prophetic authority is not born of human imagination, but of the commission and word of the Lord.

outline.title: Condemnation of the prophets who invent their messages
outline.explanation: God commands Ezekiel to denounce the prophets of Israel who prophesy on their own initiative. They are called fools because they follow their own spirit, they were not sent by God, and yet they speak as if they had received revelation. The image of the prophets as foxes in the deserts points out that, instead of protecting the people, they exploit the ruins and leave the gaps without repair. The result is judgment: God opposes them, removes their credibility and excludes them from the fate of his people.

outline.title: The poorly built wall and the illusion of peace
outline.explanation: The prophets fed the deception by saying "Peace!" when there was no peace, and thus covered with weak plaster a unstable wall. The metaphor shows that the apparent solidity of the community was false because there was no real repentance or faithfulness. When the storm sent by God comes, the structure will fall and its fragile foundation will fall and be exposed. Thus, the false security message does not prevent judgment; rather, it prepares the public collapse of the lie.

outline.title: Condemnation of the prophetess who hunt souls
outline.explanation: The denunciation extends to the women who prophesied from their own hearts and used ritual signs to arrest people, such as those who hunt birds. They defiled God among the people in exchange for small earnings, reversing good and evil: they grinded the righteous and encouraged the wicked. God promises to tear up his devices, deliver his people from their hands and make them completely cease. The outcome reaffirms that the liberation of the people comes from the action of God, not from religious manipulation.

study.context: The chapter addresses the people of Israel amid a time of national crisis and threat of judgment. The text mentions Jerusalem and the land of Israel, and presupposes a scenario in which security messages were popular, although without basis in God's word. The notes also suggest that some false prophets were in Jerusalem and others among the exiles, but the chapter emphasizes above all its liar message and its destructive effect. The language of construction, storm and capture expresses the fragility of false hope before the divine judgment.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that true revelation belongs to God and not to human religious initiative. Prophecy without divine submission is a lie, even if you use the name of the LORD. God not only rejects the false content; he judges the messengers to distort his word and oppress the people. It is also clear that the peace promised by these agents was a peace without repentance, without truth and unfounded. Theologically, the text unites holiness and mercy: God exposes the deception to deliver his people from him. There is also an important moral principle: religious lies can hurt the righteous and encourage the wicked, so the Lord acts to undo such a deception and restore responsibility before him.

scholarViews.insight: The decisive difference between the true and the false prophets is that they invented their own messages; therefore the judgment announced against them is also God's answer to the deception that spread.

The false prophets are particularly severely reproved because, under the appearance of comfort, they caused the greatest harm to the people and confronted God directly in promising peace without real basis.
The expression about speaking of one's hearts describes people who were neither inspired nor sent by God, but took on to themselves the prophetic mission by presumption.

questions: What practical signs distinguish a message that comes from God from a message that just pleases the ear?
In what ways can the promise of "peace" become a disguise for the absence of repentance and obedience?
How can God's people protect the righteous from being discouraged and the wicked from being confirmed in error?
study.practice: Examine with serious every religious message you receive: is it aligned with the word of God, call repentance and produce faithfulness, or just offer superficial relief? In dealing with others, avoid repeating spiritual promises without biblical foundation. Instead, cultivate a true, humble and responsible speech that does not manipulate consciences. It is also a call to support leaders and teachers who do not speak of themselves, but serve Scripture faithfully.
study.uncertainty: The chapter uses strong images and, at some points, its metaphor is not entirely explicit in the text itself. The notes provided help to identify the general sense, but do not allow us to state with certainty additional historical details about specific people, exact places or ritualistic practices beyond what the text mentions. The image of the prophetess in 13:18 can be understood in complementary ways in the notes; therefore, the description was maintained at the safe level of religious manipulation and capture of people.
